note: The final keynote for the Grand Jury Round (14 Oct 2026), one entry per slide of Sahayak_Keynote_v5.pptx: about five and a half minutes of talk at a calm pace, then two minutes where the jury tries the app on their phones or on the laptop, then questions. The deck's speaker notes (docs/deck/build_deck_keynote.js, matched by slide name) and the script page are both built from this file. A step is either a DO (an action, never spoken) or a SAY (spoken by I = Ishmiit or R = Roshan). Each new line in a SAY is a pause. Nothing in it assumes the jury saw an earlier round.

slides.name: The message
slides.show: The scam SMS, large, as a phone shows it: Hindi, with the English below.

steps.do: Before you walk on: the deck is on slide 1. Nothing in your hands but the clicker.
Walk to the centre and stop. Look at the jury. Say nothing until the room is quiet.

steps.say:
It’s nine at night, and a phone buzzes.
You can read it for yourself.
Her account closes tonight, unless she updates her KYC.
And there’s a link.

slides.name: Who reads it
slides.show: Four words, one per line: 74. 9 PM. Bank closed. Alone.

steps.do: Click.

steps.say:
Now picture who’s holding that phone.
She’s seventy-four. Her bank shut hours ago.
Her son is in another city.
Whatever she does next, she decides alone.

slides.name: Every minute
slides.show: “₹4 lakh”, lost to cyber fraud every minute, on average. Below: ₹22,495 crore in 2025, and ₹4,005 crore of it from senior citizens.

steps.do: Click. Say nothing for two seconds. Let the number sit.

steps.say:
She isn’t one story. She’s millions.
Last year, Indians reported losing over twenty-two thousand crore rupees to cyber fraud.
That’s about four lakh rupees every minute, on average.

slides.name: Introducing Sahayak
slides.show: Sahayak, its two promises, three short pills (CSC and phone, offline, 22 languages), and the app’s home screen.

steps.do: Click. Take one step toward the jury.

steps.say:
So we built her a helper.
It’s called Sahayak, and it does two things.
It catches the scam before the money moves.
And it finds what she’s owed.

At the Common Services Centre in her village, or on her own phone, even offline.
And every screen, every answer, comes in all twenty-two of India’s scheduled languages.
Good morning. I’m Ishmiit Singh, and this is Roshan Raj.

steps.do: On Roshan’s name, open a hand toward Roshan. Roshan nods.

slides.name: It tells her why
slides.show: Sahayak’s answer to that SMS on a phone, “Scam.”, and six short cues: three reasons, three things to do.

steps.do: Click.

steps.say:
Back to her message.
She pastes it in, and in under a second:
Scam.

But a warning people don’t understand gets ignored.
So Sahayak tells her why, in plain words.
A bank won’t text from a personal number. That link only pretends to be SBI’s.
And what to do: don’t tap, keep the message as proof, and if money’s gone, call 1930.

slides.name: What she is owed
slides.show: “₹5 lakh” of free hospital care a year, three short cues, and Sahayak’s benefits result for a 74-year-old.

steps.do: Click.

steps.say:
And building this, something surprised us.
The people scammers chase are often missing out on what’s already theirs.

At seventy-four, she’s entitled to free hospital care, up to five lakh rupees a year, whatever her income.
Yet by February, fewer than one in five people over seventy had the card.

So Sahayak asks five simple questions, puts that card first,
and gives her the exact sentence to say at the counter.

slides.name: How it works
slides.show: Three cards with a few words each: You ask. Rules decide. A clear answer. Below: phone and counter agree, 1,841 of 1,841.

steps.do: Click.

steps.say:
She can type, speak, describe a call, or photograph a UPI QR code.
Sixty-four scam signals run right on the device, so nothing she types leaves her phone.

She gets one of four answers, and ‘safe’ isn’t one of them.
Because no one can promise that.

slides.name: Why rules decide
slides.show: A 3B language model against Sahayak on the same 137 real messages. Roshan speaks.

steps.do: Click.

steps.say:
Now, you might ask: why not just let an AI model decide?
We asked that too. So we tested one.
Roshan.

steps.do: Turn to Roshan and step back. Roshan steps forward.

steps.say: On the same hundred and thirty-seven real messages, it caught more scams than we did.

But it called twenty-one of thirty-four genuine messages a scam. We did that eleven times.
A warning that cries wolf gets ignored.
So rules decide, and every answer says why.
Thank you, Roshan.

slides.name: The honest number
slides.show: “7 in 10” on 137 real messages, scored once, with the two bigger numbers greyed out on the left.

steps.do: Click.

steps.say:
On messages we wrote ourselves, Sahayak caught thirty-four of thirty-seven.
But real messages are harder.

On a hundred and thirty-seven that people in India actually received, scored once, it caught seven in ten.
That’s the number we stand behind.

slides.name: The pilot
slides.show: One district: 20 villages, 50 counters, six months, and ₹25–35k for a CSC’s computer, once. The next 30 days.

steps.do: Click.

steps.say:
So, the pilot.
One district. Twenty villages. Fifty counters. Six months.
Each CSC needs one computer, twenty-five to thirty-five thousand rupees, once.
After that, every check costs nothing.

slides.name: The ask
slides.show: “Introduce us to one district.” Above it: 6 lakh CSCs, and the 50 counters we need.

steps.do: Click. Stop moving. Look at the head juror.

steps.say:
And that’s where you come in.
India has six lakh Common Services Centres.
We need fifty counters.

Introduce us to one district.
One morning to start, then six months.
And we’ll come back with real numbers, from real people.

slides.name: One more thing
slides.show: Spot the scam: the game on the Learn tab. Two phones: a card (Scam or real?) and Sahayak’s clues after the answer.

steps.do: Click. Pause. Take one step toward the jury.

steps.say:
And, one more thing.
The best defence is spotting a scam before it arrives.
So we built a game. Spot the scam.
You’ll play it in a minute.

slides.name: Someone to ask
slides.show: Nine at night. Now she has someone to ask. Sahayak, its two promises, and both your names.

steps.do: Click.

steps.say:
So, back to her, one last time.
Nine at night. The bank is closed. The link is right there.
But now, before she taps, she has someone to ask.

Sahayak.
Spot the scam before the money moves.
Claim what you’re owed.

slides.name: Try it yourself
slides.show: The deck’s only QR code, and four things to try. The jury explores the app on their phones or on the laptop.

steps.do: Click.

steps.say:
But please, don’t take our word for it.
Scan this code, and Sahayak opens on your phone.
Nothing to install. No account.
Or, if you’d rather watch, Roshan will show you on our laptop.

Try a scam message, ask what a seventy-four-year-old is owed, or switch to your own language.
And turn on airplane mode. It still works.

steps.do: Hands-on, about two minutes. Roshan drives the app on the laptop (it is on the screen behind you): the Ayushman ₹500 scam, ‘What am I owed?’ as a 74-year-old, a switch to Tamil, the Learn tab, and the new game. Ishmiit walks the demo phone to any juror whose phone won’t scan. Answer what they ask as they try it; keep it short.
When the first juror looks up, or at two minutes: step back to the centre.

steps.say:
Thank you.
Roshan and I would love to take your questions.

steps.do: Roshan steps to the centre for the questions. Ishmiit stays on stage, half a step back.
